counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If comparable corpora are moderately large (≥~2M tokens) and alignments/phrase tables provide sufficiently accurate dictionaries (~5K reliable pairs), linear mapping will align entity-bearing vectors well enough for English NER to generalize.
If projected entity labels exhibit consistent tagging errors only rarely, frequency-based q(y) will successfully prioritize correct sentences and improve AP.

If AP and RP confidences maintain systematic differences (AP precision >> RP recall) across languages, rank-based co-decoding will reliably increase F1 by boosting recall without large precision loss.

If mapping dictionaries are high-quality and cover common entity surface forms (names, locations), representation projection will transfer semantics needed for NER even across related and moderately distant languages.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper assembles known components (annotation projection, embedding mapping) with pragmatic heuristics (q(y)/n(y), weighted linear mapping, two co-decoding heuristics) to produce a practical system showing empirical gains; contributions are useful engineering advances rather than paradigm shifts.
evidence: Use of frequency-based selection and weighted linear mapping are concrete heuristics built on prior ideas.
Empirical improvements over baselines and prior work on CoNLL dev/test and in-house data.
uncertainty_flags: Generality of heuristics across different resource regimes and languages is not fully verified.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applying a sentence-level frequency table q(y) for selecting projection-labeled sentences from comparable corpora and directly mapping arbitrary target embeddings into English to apply an English NER decoder together, then fusing them with simple rank heuristics, is a combination less commonly found in prior work and may offer a practical new recipe for zero-resource NER.
evidence: Paper claims and demonstrates complementary behavior and successful fusion across multiple languages, including fine-grained in-house types.
Prior work cited (Täckström, Tsai) uses different approaches (clusters, wikification), so the concrete AP+RP+co-decoding pipeline fills a gap.
uncertainty_flags: Risk that novelty stems from clever engineering tuned for available corpora rather than robustly generalizable methodological novelty.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately to highly confident that the paper's empirical claims are supported for the datasets and resources used (evidence: multiple tables showing consistent patterns). Uncertainty remains about generalization across resource-poor languages, stability under hyperparameter variation, mapping alternatives, and calibration; these gaps reduce the upper bound of confidence.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a practical two-view cross-lingual NER pipeline: annotation projection (AP) with a sentence-level data-selection heuristic (q(y), n), representation-projection (RP) via a weighted linear mapping of target embeddings into an English space, and two lightweight co-decoding fusion heuristics (exclude-O confidence-based and rank-priority).

Empirical results on the reported in-house and CoNLL datasets show that (a) data-selection substantially improves AP when alignment quality is low (notably Japanese and Korean in the paper), (b) the linear weighted mapping enables direct application of an English neural NER to target languages producing usable results, and (c) co-decoding heuristics typically increase F1 relative to either AP or RP alone and beat the cited prior baselines in the reported settings.
The manuscript provides concrete, implementable recipes (explicit equations, algorithmic rules) that are reproducible in principle given comparable resources and sufficient implementation detail.
NN2 (the prototype-based smoothing variant) often increases recall compared to NN1 and can change the precision/recall trade-off, although its effect is dataset- and language-dependent.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: some reviewers view the work as an engineering/incremental refinement of known ideas (annotation projection + embedding mapping + heuristics), whereas others view the specific combination (sentence-level frequency selection on comparable corpora + weighted mapping + co-decoding) as a potentially useful innovation signal. The disagreement is about perceived novelty significance, not about empirical results.

Sufficiency of linear mapping: reviewers differ on whether restricting to the presented unconstrained weighted linear mapping is acceptable as a default (some consider it plausible and pragmatic), while others see lacking comparisons to orthogonal/Procrustes or nonlinear mappings as a major omission.

Approach generality: reviewers agree results hold on the reported languages/resources but disagree on how strongly to generalize claims. Some interpret the experiments as adequate evidence of broad applicability (conditional on similar resources), others consider portability to truly low-resource or typologically distant languages insufficiently supported.

Importance of co-decoding design: reviewers concur co-decoding helps in the reported experiments, but disagree on whether the presented heuristics are an adequate, general solution vs. a potentially brittle, dev-tuned patch needing calibration or learned fusion alternatives.
uncertainty_hotspots: Per-language hyperparameter tuning (q, n, choice of co-decoding variant): It is unclear how sensitive performance is to these choices and whether per-language tuning is required to achieve reported gains.

Mapping method and dictionary dependence: Uncertainty about whether the weighted unconstrained linear map and the chosen ~5K-6K dictionary size are broadly optimal; no ablation against orthogonal, constrained linear, or nonlinear mappings and limited evidence on dictionary-size sensitivity.

Confidence calibration across heterogeneous systems: Co-decoding uses confidence values from different models (AP MEMM vs RP NN) but no calibration diagnostics are reported; this affects the reliability and portability of the exclude-O confidence fusion.

Resource assumptions and low-resource applicability: Both AP and RP rely on comparable corpora, alignment/phrase tables, and decent monolingual corpora for embeddings; how performance degrades with smaller/noisier resources is not quantified.

Statistical robustness: Reported results are single-point estimates without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests; reported gains (especially modest ones) might be within experimental variability.

Validity of frequency-as-trust assumption: The sentence-quality score q(y) assumes frequently projected tags for an entity indicate correctness; if projection errors are systematic, q(y) could prefer consistent but incorrect labels.
model_diversity_effects: Complementarity exploited: Across reviewers there is consistent recognition that AP and RP produce different error profiles (AP tends to be higher-precision/low-recall; RP tends to be more balanced), and that exploiting this diversity via co-decoding yields empirical improvements.

Calibration and comparability issues: Diversity of system types (sequence-labeling via projection-trained MEMM vs. neural decoder on mapped embeddings) introduces heterogeneity in scoring and confidence distributions; this heterogeneity creates both an opportunity (complementary strengths) and a risk (incomparable confidences that complicate naive fusion).

Dependency on resource-induced diversity: The practical benefit of combining the two models depends on the extent to which their error modes are uncorrelated; when both systems make correlated mistakes (e.g., due to domain mismatch or shared projection biases), fusion gains may shrink or reverse.

Role-specific effects: AP's effectiveness is strongly influenced by alignment quality and sentence-selection filtering, while RP's effectiveness is sensitive to dictionary coverage and embedding alignment — these role-specific dependencies mean model diversity effects will vary across languages and resource regimes.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Use the paper as an engineering/methodological contribution that demonstrates a practical, reproducible pipeline for zero-target-label cross-lingual NER under certain resource assumptions. When taking editorial action, center decisions on whether the paper provides sufficient empirical and methodological validation for its claims rather than on an aggregate novelty score. Key editorial considerations and required improvements before broader generalization: (1) require sensitivity and ablation analyses for core hyperparameters (q, n, dictionary size, embedding dimensions) to demonstrate robustness and to reduce per-language tuning dependence; (2) require statistical-robustness reporting (multiple runs, standard deviations or bootstrap confidence intervals, and significance tests against baselines) for key comparisons; (3) request experiments or controlled simulations showing behavior under reduced-resource settings (smaller comparable corpora or smaller/noisier dictionaries) or explicit discussion of applicability limits if experiments are infeasible; (4) require evaluation of mapping alternatives (orthogonal/Procrustes and at least one simple nonlinear variant) or justification why linear weighted mapping suffices; (5) request calibration analysis of model confidences and comparison with a simple learned fusion baseline (stacking or calibration) to show co-decoding heuristics are not merely dev-set artifacts. The editor should treat the reported empirical wins as valid for the resources used but insist on added analyses or clearer caveats before allowing broad claims of generalizability.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewers' concerns, provide the following revisions and additional analyses: (1) Sensitivity ablations: show performance sweeps for q and n (F1 vs selected training size), dictionary size (e.g., 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K), and embedding dimension variations; include at least two representative languages (one close to English and one typologically-distant) to illustrate trends. (2) Mapping variants: compare the current weighted linear mapping to orthogonal-constrained mapping (Procrustes), unweighted linear mapping, and a small nonlinear mapping (e.g., 1-hidden-layer MLP) to quantify whether linearity is sufficient. (3) Confidence calibration: provide calibration diagnostics (reliability diagrams or expected calibration error) for AP and RP confidences; evaluate whether simple calibration (temperature scaling) or a small learned combiner on dev data outperforms the exclude-O and rank heuristics. (4) Statistical robustness: run key experiments with multiple random seeds and/or bootstrap the test sets; report mean and standard deviation (or confidence intervals) and conduct paired significance tests versus baselines for the main claims. (5) Resource-dependence analysis: either run experiments simulating reduced resources (downsample comparable corpora and phrase tables) or add an explicit discussion and limitations section detailing expected behavior in low-resource regimes. (6) Reproducibility: include a hyperparameter appendix listing all important settings (NN2 prototype count and initialization, embedding training regimes, alignment and phrase-table extraction parameters, q/n search ranges, dev-set selection protocol) and, if possible, release code or scripts to reproduce data-extraction and mapping steps. (7) Diagnostic validation: empirically validate that q(y) correlates with true sentence-level labeling accuracy on a small held-out annotated sample, and report failure cases where frequency-based selection prefers consistently wrong labels.

Partially provided: embedding dimensionalities, some training epoch counts, and a stated heuristic for dictionary size (~5K-6K pairs). Co-decoding heuristics are described and empirically demonstrated.

Missing or incomplete: no reported variance estimates or statistical significance testing; limited or no ablation studies for mapping alternatives (orthogonal, nonlinear), dictionary-size sensitivity, or q/n sensitivity curves; insufficient calibration analysis of confidence scores; limited documentation of NN2 prototype hyperparameters (count, initialization, training details); incomplete details on alignment and phrase-table extraction parameters and preprocessing scripts.

Reproducibility risk: per-language tuned hyperparameters and dev-selected co-decoding variants increase the difficulty of replication without full dev-protocol and hyperparameter lists; releasing code and exact data-extraction parameters would mitigate these risks.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis and judgments above are constrained to the information extracted from the provided shared analysis and specialist reviews. I do not have access to the full paper text, appendices, or raw data/code; therefore I cannot verify unreported ablations, full numeric tables (e.g., the referenced Table 5), or whether the authors already included some requested analyses. Empirical claims are accepted conditionally: reviewers consistently confirm the reported improvements on the specific datasets and resources used, but generalization to other corpora, languages (especially truly low-resource or typologically distant ones), alternative mapping methods, or settings with different alignment and phrase-table qualities remains uncertain. The assessments of novelty and risk mix objective evidence (reported tables/equations) with interpretative judgments about sufficiency of validation; where reviewers disagree (degree of novelty, sufficiency of linear mapping), I preserve the controlled disagreement rather than resolving it. Finally, numerical extents of improvements may be sensitive to randomness and resource choices; absence of variance information limits confidence in fine-grained comparisons.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The paper presents a practical pipeline for zero-target-language-label cross-lingual NER that combines (1) annotation projection (AP) from English into comparable corpora with a sentence-level frequency-based data-selection metric q(y) and minimum entity count n(y); (2) representation-projection (RP) that learns a weighted linear map from target to English embedding space (using ~5K–6K phrase-table-derived pairs) to apply an English neural NER directly; and (3) two lightweight co-decoding heuristics (exclude-O confidence and rank-priority) to fuse AP and RP outputs. Experiments on several languages (in-house fine-grained and CoNLL tasks) show: large AP gains from data selection when alignment is poor (Japanese/Korean), usable RP transfer via linear mapping (NN1/NN2), and consistent F1 improvements from co-decoding over single-view baselines and cited prior work in the reported setups.
strengths: Concrete, implementable algorithms: explicit eqns for sentence score q(y) and weighted linear mapping (Eq.5/7) plus fully described co-decoding rules.
Empirical breadth: evaluations on multiple languages/datasets (in-house fine-grained types and CoNLL) showing consistent patterns (AP benefits from selection; RP provides complementary recall).
Insightful system framing: treats AP and RP as complementary views and demonstrates practical fusion strategies that leverage this complementarity.
Pragmatic engineering focus: resource-aware design choices (dictionary-size heuristics, MEMM/NN trade-offs) suited to large-vocabulary NER in weakly supervised regimes.
limitations: Per-language hyperparameter dependence: key parameters (q, n, co-decoding variant selection, dictionary size, embedding dims, NN2 prototype settings) are tuned per language with no systematic sensitivity analyses or cross-language defaults demonstrated; this raises overfitting/portability concerns.

Limited mapping-method ablation: representation-projection is restricted to an unconstrained weighted linear map; no comparisons to orthogonal/Procrustes, unweighted variants, or simple nonlinear mappings are reported, leaving uncertainty about linearity sufficiency for typologically distant languages.

Confidence-calibration gap for fusion: co-decoding uses confidences from heterogeneous systems (AP MEMM vs RP NN) but lacks calibration diagnostics (reliability diagrams, ECE) or comparison to learned fusion (stacker), so the exclude-O heuristic may be brittle outside tuned dev settings.

Statistical robustness and reproducibility omissions: reported P/R/F1 are point estimates without variance (multiple runs/bootstrap CIs) or significance testing; some hyperparameter and preprocessing details (NN2 prototype counts/initialization, phrase-table extraction parameters, dev-tuning protocol) are incompletely specified.
open_questions: How sensitive are the AP gains to the exact (q,n) choices? Please provide F1 vs q/n sweeps (or at least curves) for representative languages and indicate recommended defaults when no dev set is available.

How does the weighted linear mapping compare to orthogonal-constrained (Procrustes) mapping, unweighted linear mapping, and a small nonlinear mapper (MLP) on at least one close and one distant language? Provide ablation results.

Are AP and RP confidence scores calibrated comparably? Provide calibration diagnostics (reliability diagrams or ECE) and test whether simple calibration (temperature scaling) or a small learned combiner improves over exclude-O/rank heuristics.

How do results degrade with reduced resources? Report experiments (or simulated downsampling) showing performance when the comparable corpus and/or phrase-table dictionary are much smaller or noisier.

Does q(y) correlate with sentence-level true label accuracy? Please report the empirical correlation on a small held-out annotated sample and examples of where q(y) selects consistently wrong labels (failure cases).
What are NN2 prototype hyperparameters (count, initialization, regularization) and how sensitive are RP results to embedding dimensionality choices (e.g., English 300d vs targets 800d)?
consensus_snapshot: AP with sentence-level data selection (q(y), n) substantially improves projection-based NER when alignment quality is low (empirical support: Japanese/Korean gains).

Representation-projection via a weighted linear mapping permits direct use of an English NN decoder and yields complementary error profiles (often higher recall / more balanced P/R), as demonstrated across languages.
Co-decoding heuristics that combine AP and RP outputs typically increase F1 over either approach alone in the reported experiments.
The paper provides clear, implementable recipes valuable as an engineering baseline for zero-resource cross-lingual NER under the assumed resource conditions.
disagreement_snapshot: Novelty valuation: some reviewers view the contribution as incremental engineering (combining known components with pragmatic tweaks), while others see the specific combination (frequency-based sentence selection on comparable corpora + weighted mapping + co-decoding) as a useful innovation signal — the disagreement concerns significance rather than empirical validity on reported data.

Sufficiency of linear mapping: reviewers diverge on whether the unconstrained weighted linear map is an acceptable default; some expect comparisons to orthogonal or nonlinear mappings as essential, others accept the pragmatic choice conditional on resource assumptions.

Generalizability: reviewers agree reported gains hold for the used corpora/languages but differ on how strongly to generalize to truly low-resource or typologically distant languages without further experiments.
uncertainty_snapshot: Effect sizes may be sensitive to per-language tuning and the particular comparable corpora and phrase-tables used — absence of variance/CI prevents assessing robustness of reported numeric gains.
Calibration of confidence outputs across heterogeneous models is untested; co-decoding gains might partially reflect score incomparabilities exploitable on dev data but not necessarily transferable.

Linear mapping optimality is unsettled: its performance likely depends on dictionary coverage, embedding training regimes, and language distance; lacking ablation creates uncertainty about portability.
q(y) frequency-as-trust assumption could favor systematic but incorrect projections when source NER/alignment errors are biased; empirical diagnostics of this risk are absent.

Required revisions: (1) sensitivity ablations for q/n and dictionary size (representative languages), (2) mapping method comparisons (orthogonal/Procrustes and at least one nonlinear baseline), (3) calibration diagnostics and comparison to a learned fusion baseline or simple calibration, (4) variance reporting (multiple runs or bootstrap CIs) and significance testing for main comparisons, (5) resource-dependence analysis or explicit discussion/limitation section if experiments are infeasible, and (6) fuller reproducibility materials (hyperparameter appendix, code/data-extraction scripts). These steps will mitigate main uncertainty hotspots and clarify the contribution's scope.

(2) Ablation comparing weighted linear mapping to orthogonal (Procrustes), unweighted linear, and a small MLP on at least two representative language pairs. (3) Calibration analysis for AP and RP confidences (reliability diagrams, ECE) and an experiment showing whether temperature scaling or a small stacking classifier on dev outperforms the current heuristics. (4) Multiple-run results (mean ± std) or bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests for key comparisons (co-decoding vs best single view and vs cited baselines). (5) Experiments or controlled downsampling showing performance degradation when comparable corpora or dictionaries are reduced, or an explicit limitation discussion if experiments cannot be run. (6) A reproducibility appendix listing all hyperparameters (NN2 prototype counts/initialization, embedding training details, alignment/phrase-table extraction parameters, q/n grid search ranges, random seeds) and consider releasing code and mapping dictionaries.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper proposes a pragmatic two-view pipeline for zero-target-label cross-lingual NER: sentence-level frequency-based selection for annotation projection, weighted linear embedding mapping for direct English-NN transfer, and two simple co-decoding heuristics to fuse outputs. Empirical results on several languages/datasets indicate substantial AP gains from selection when alignment is poor, usable RP transfer, and regular F1 improvements from co-decoding.

Strengths: Concrete algorithms and equations (q(y), weighted mapping), broad multilingual experiments (in-house fine-grained and CoNLL), clear identification of complementary error profiles (AP high-precision, RP more balanced), and practical engineering choices aimed at real-world weak-supervision constraints.

Limitations: (1) Many hyperparameters are tuned per language (q,n, co-decoder selection, dictionary size, embedding dims, NN2 prototype settings) with no systematic sensitivity or cross-language transfer analysis. (2) Representation-projection explores only a weighted linear map; no comparisons to orthogonal/constrained or nonlinear mapping alternatives are provided. (3) Co-decoding relies on comparing confidences across heterogeneous weak systems but lacks calibration diagnostics or comparison to learned fusion, potentially making the heuristics brittle. (4) Results are reported as single point estimates without variance or significance testing and some implementation/preprocessing details (e.g., NN2 prototype specifics, phrase-table extraction thresholds) are incompletely specified.

Open Questions: (1) How stable are AP gains across q/n choices—please include F1 vs q/n curves and recommended defaults for no-dev scenarios? (2) How does weighted linear mapping compare to Procrustes/orthogonal or simple nonlinear mappings on representative language pairs? (3) Are AP and RP confidences calibrated? Provide calibration plots and test temperature scaling or a small dev-trained combiner vs exclude-O/rank heuristics. (4) How does performance change when comparable corpora or dictionaries are downsampled/noisier? (5) Does q(y) correlate with true sentence-level label accuracy—please report correlation and failure-case examples. (6) What are NN2 prototype hyperparameters and sensitivity to embedding dims?

Transparency: The paper includes explicit algorithmic formulations and per-language results but should add variance reporting, ablation studies (mapping alternatives, dictionary size, q/n sensitivity), calibration diagnostics, and a reproducibility appendix (hyperparameters, seeds, preprocessing/mapping scripts). Releasing code and mapping dictionaries would substantially improve reproducibility.

confidence_interval.rationale: High confidence that the methods produce the reported empirical improvements on the provided datasets and resources (multiple reviewers observed consistent table patterns). Moderate confidence that the pipeline is a useful engineering baseline. Lower confidence in claims of broad generalizability because core uncertainties remain (per-language tuning, mapping alternatives, calibration, resource dependence, and lack of variance/ significance reporting). The interval reflects strong internal validity for the reported settings but substantial epistemic uncertainty about portability beyond them.
